paragraphs: My name is Tom, and I am twelve years old. On Saturday, Dad had a bad headache. I went with him and Lily to the chemist near the market. The woman gave Dad a small box. "Please read the label first," she said. I read it to Dad. It said, "For a headache: one tablet after food." Under that, it said, "Only for adults and children over twelve." "I am only twelve, so this is not for me," I said. "Do you want anything else?" asked the woman.

Next to the chemist, there was a toy shop. Lily wanted a present for Pat's birthday, so we went into the toy shop. She found a red box with two toy cars. The label said, "Fast Cars. For ages six and over." "Pat is eight, so this is good for him," said Lily. On the bottom, it said, "Batteries are not in the box." "We must buy batteries too," I said. "Look, there is a repair kit in the box," said Lily. "Pat can repair a car if a wheel comes off."

At home, I wanted to wear my blue T-shirt for the school race. It was dirty, so I looked at the label. The label was inside the neck. The first line said, "Size M." The second line said, "Wash in cold water." The third line said, "Do not use a hot iron." The last line said, "Dry in the shade." I washed the T-shirt in cold water. Then I put it in the shade.

That night, I thought about the labels of the day. A label gives us the key facts. We can read it in one minute. Dad took his tablet after food. In the evening, his headache was better. Pat liked his fast cars, and the batteries worked well. Labels help us every day. "Did you read the label?" is a good question for every box.
text.summary: Tom reads four labels in one day. A medicine box, a toy box, and a T-shirt label all give him key facts.
